The Kuamut Rainforest Conservation Project (‘Kuamut Project’) aims to protect and restore 83,381 ha of 
tropical forest in Sabah, Malaysia. The project is located in the Tongod and Kinabatangan Districts of 
Sabah, Malaysia. The project area is part of a long-term approximately 1-million-hectare concession 
granted to Yayasan Sabah on a 99-year lease arrangement with the Sabah Forestry Department (acting on 
behalf of the State Government of Sabah). Yayasan Sabah is a State-owned para-governmental charitable 
foundation that was formed in 1966 with the aim of ‘improving the lives of Malaysians living in Sabah’.

Prior to the start of the project, the project area was designated as production forest (Class II). The area 
had been repeatedly logged in the past and was designated for further commercial exploitation. Project 
additionality is explicitly demonstrated by preventing continued commercial logging and instead manage 
the area for protection. Had the project not intervened, the resulting carbon emissions over this period 
would have contributed 16,291,488.57 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent (tCO2e) to the atmosphere in 
the period 2016 – 2045, equivalent to an annual average of 543,049 tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent 
(tCO2e).

In addition to its contribution to preventing the release of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, the project is 
protecting an important biodiverse habitat. Despite its ex-logged state, the area is known to support very 
high populations of elephants, banteng and orangutan, and endangered bird species including Helmeted 
Hornbill, Bornean Peacock Pheasant and Storms Stork. The project will also improve the conditions for 
communities by improving access to water quality though the restoration of riparian reserves, generation of 
direct employment in project activities such as forest restoration, patrolling, etc. The project also aims to 
improve health services and reduce conflicts with outsiders working in logging concessions who would 
have arrived in the absence of the project. Furthermore, the project will provide training to community 
members to improve their skills in tourism, handicraft elaboration and improved agricultural practices as 
well as facilitate access to markets as well as formal and informal education packages, including for 
children.

Due to the history of repeated logging, the area is now a complex mosaic of forest in conditions ranging 
from intact to highly degraded. The most likely land use scenario without the project would therefore have 
been a combination of different forest management practices. Parts of the area would have been subjected 
to continued selective logging. The rest of the area would have been managed using a practice that is 
known locally as the Mosaic Planting Approach. The concept of Mosaic Planting Approach involved 
retaining small patches of natural forest areas containing young commercial tree species during harvesting, 
and planting of fast-growing species in the more open areas. The small patches of natural forests left 
standing comprise commercially forest species with a diameter below the prescribed cutting limit. The more 
open areas left are cleaned and planted with selected forest plantation species.

Hydrology: There is an extensive network of streams within the project area, most of them unnamed. 
Generally, these streams all drain into the Kuamut River, which flows through the centre of the project area.

Vegetation: The natural forests of central-eastern Sabah are dominated by dipterocarps, particularly 
Parashorea malaanonan and P. tomentella together with Shorea johorensis and other Shorea species of 
the Rubroshorea group. Between 80 and 90% of large canopy trees belong to the Depterocarpaceae with 
the balance being accounted for mainly by Koompassia, Diospyros and Durio species. Although 
dipterocarps dominate the upper canopy, understory species from families such as Euphorbiaceae and 
Rubiaceae can make up over 85% of small stems. There are clear riverine and streamside associations 
comprising smaller trees of genera including Saraca, Eugenia, Dillenia and Octomeles. Relatively few large 
palms are found in the forests of this part of Sabah. At higher elevations (above approximately 700 m) the 
canopy seldom exceeds 25m and includes the gymnosperms Agathis Phylocladus and Podocarpus spp. In 
terms of dynamics, the forests of central Sabah are thought to be in the late stages of recovery form an 
exceptionally severe drought disturbance at the end of the 19th century. Moderate to severe droughts, 
occurring irregularly at intervals of 1-2 events every 20 years, are an important feature of the forest 
environment of this part of Borneo. Tree species, particularly those in the understory, are well adapted to 
temporary water stress, the intensity of which changes along the local topographic gradient from low slopes 
to ridge tops; such stochastic variations doubtless play an important role in shorter-term forest dynamics 
and the maintenance of tree species richness. Prior to this project, research on the forests of Kuamut has 
been limited, but given their broadly similar topography, elevation, underlying geology and soils, much 
information can be derived from the adjacent and much better described Danum Valley Conservation Area 
(DVCA), the western and north-western flanks of which are fully contiguous with the Kuamut Forest 
Reserve. The knowledge of the flora of DVCA is based on general botanical collecting in the vicinity of the 
Danum Valley Field Centre including a number of WWF expeditions during the 1970s and subsequent 
much more detailed but localised enumeration studies. The higher-plant checklist compiled to date 
comprises more than 1,300 species in 562 genera of 139 families. Although this list is far from complete, it 
already represents close to 15% of the approximately 10,000 species of higher plants recorded for Sabah. 
There is no reason to assume that floral composition of the Kuamut Forest Reserve would differ 
substantively from the DVCA.

In most communities across Sabah, it is historically not uncommon for children to leave formal education 
upon the completion of primary school. This is frequently due to the distance from secondary schools (and 
the associated costs of supporting children at boarding schools) and the need for additional inputs in the 
family's agricultural production. Whilst this trend is noticeable in Keramuak and Kuamut, Figure 5 also 
indicates that rates of education are improving dramatically, with a large proportion of under 30s having 
completed secondary school and even tertiary education. This is in marked contrast with cohorts over 40, 
and the survey data indicate that the current rate of school dropouts (i.e. those who do not complete 
secondary education) is only 13.7%.

These trends are not consistent between the Keramuak and Kuamut clusters however, with a much lower 
overall proportion of adults in Kuamut having completed secondary school (13.3%) compared to adults in 
Keramuak (36.1%). This is likely to result from the more isolated location of the Kuamut villages and the 
difficulties in physical access to secondary schools, and possibly also due to lower general levels of income 
in Kuamut.

Guard posts: Guard posts will be established progressively over the first 1-3 years of the project 
and will be positioned at the main access points to the project area. Each post will be manned by 
2-4 staff working on rotation and will be equipped with all required facilities and satellite 
phone/radio as required. It is expected to establish at least 5 posts in the first years which will 
require 10 to 20 full time staff. All observations will be recorded, and access will be limited to 
those permitted to enter the project area legitimately. In addition to these guard posts, project 
offices will be opened in each of the two main village groups (Kuamut and Karamuak) to facilitate 
the community development program (see below) and to encourage community participation, 
collaboration and employment in the site protection work and patrolling.

Patrolling and monitoring: In addition to static guard posts, the project will undertake routine 
monitoring along major road and river access routes by car/motorbike and boat as required. Staff 
will also undertake periodic foot patrols, particularly along remote access points in the north 
where the project area borders state land. Patrol teams will be teams of 2-3 staff, supported by 
locally hired community team members. In total, it is expected to employ 20 to 30 staff for 
patrolling activities. Each will be equipped with GPS, camera and sat phone/radio as required. 
Initially the number of permeant patrol staff will be kept low, but the number will be progressively 
increased as the project develops. Permanent teams will also be supplemented by temporary 
additional staff as required. Where possible, routine or periodic patrolling will be combined with 
biodiversity and carbon survey work for cost-effectiveness.

As described above, the project-zone communities only have close access to very basic health care. The 
Kuamut Project will seek to improve this by working closely with local government to improve access to 
public services and to assist local government in providing health education at the village level. Through 
project implementation, community members will be allowed to access to the health services established 
for the project team onsite. The Kuamut Project will also seek to improve local sanitation practices, 
including the common practice of discharge of all waste into local rivers, which are in turn used for cooking, 
drinking and bathing. The Kuamut Project will work with the villages together with local government 
agencies to bring awareness about and improve sanitation in each village, increase access to clean 
drinking water, and develop waste treatment facilities in each village. A more detailed analysis will be 
conducted through project implementation to potentially support the installation of piped water for the 
communities in the Kuamut cluster.

In regard to improving education, the Kuamut Project aims to support the local government’s efforts to 
improve the quality of basic education and the number of enrolment and encourage the youth to pursue 
higher education. The project will implement an open competitive scholarship program to provide funding to 
selected students and will assist to develop facilities at local schools. Capacity building and educational 
workshops for teachers will be conducted as well through various training programs.

are thus additional ethical considerations at the present time with respect to minimizing risks of community 
exposure to Coronavirus.

For the above reasons, by the time of validation the project will need to re-establish engagements with

In accordance with the methodology, the steps in VCS tool VT0001 were considered as a stepwise 
approach for justifying the selection and determination of the most plausible baseline scenario. In order to 
determine the most likely baseline scenario a barrier analysis (step 3 in VT0001) was applied to determine 
which of the scenarios from step 1 is the most likely baseline scenario.

For scenario i. (palm oil), barriers exist consisting of barriers related to local ecological conditions and 
technological barriers. The barriers related to the local ecological conditions have to do with the fact that 
the conditions in the project area, especially when it comes to soils and topography (slopes), are sub-
optimal for establishing large scale industrial palm oil plantations. Although this hasn’t always stopped the 
establishment of palm oil plantations in other areas, in the case of the project area there are additional 
technological barriers since the area is relatively far removed from suitable roads and milling facilities, 
making it unattractive to develop palm oil plantations in the project area. The combination of these barriers 
would have prevented scenario i. from occurring.

Scenario ii. would be a continuation of the current land use. The main barriers for this scenario to apply to 
the whole project area are technological and local ecological conditions. More specifically, due to the 
history of repeated logging, the area is now a complex mosaic of forest in conditions ranging from intact to 
highly degraded. Especially the areas with highly degraded forest are commercially not very attractive due 
to low levels of merchantable volume stocking and their potential for commercial regeneration. Current 
standards in Sabah for natural forest management expect a minimum of about 9 harvestable trees with a 
DBH > 60 cm per hectare for an economic attractive cut. Due to the past harvesting, parts of the project 
area are unlikely to meet this criterion, meaning the area would not produce an economic harvest without 
some form of silvicultural intervention.

The barriers that have been identified for scenario ii. have led to the development of an integrated mosaic 
planting approach (scenario iii) that is being applied in other areas controlled by Yayasan Sabah. This 
approach combines the cultivation of fast-growing trees in small blocks that are scattered among patches 
of natural forest, thereby forming a forest mosaic. Ecological conditions again are a barrier for preventing 
this scenario being rolled out in the whole project area. The mosaic planting approach is mostly applied in 
areas with slopes < 20 degrees. The topography of the project area is such that the mosaic planting 
approach cannot be applied in the whole project area, therefore preventing the implementation of scenario 
iii.

Scenario v is a scenario where the project activity of converting the area to a protected forest would be 
performed without being registered as the VCS AFOLU project. This scenario faces financial barriers. 
Yayasan Sabah’s objective is to promote economic opportunities for the people of Sabah and converting 
the area to a protected forest would generate no income, therefore making it economically and financially 
less attractive than the other land use scenarios without the revenue from the sale of GHG credits is.

Scenario iv. is a mix of scenario ii. and iii. It would allow to overcome the barriers associated with scenarios 
ii. and iii. In this scenario, Natural Forest Management and the Mosaic Planting Approach would be 
combined to allow for optimal commercial use of the forest in the project area. There are no barriers 
preventing this scenario from occurring and therefore scenario iv. (combination of Natural Forest 
Management and the Mosaic Planting Approach) is considered as the most likely baseline scenario for this 
project. In accordance with the applicability conditions of the methodology, this is a baseline scenario of 
planned timber harvest.

As shown in the previous step, the baseline scenario is one of planned timber harvest combination of 
selective logging (Natural Forest Management) and the relatively new Mosaic Planting Approach. The 
methodology requires that the project proponent must determine how to model the baseline management 
scenario with a choice between two options: a Historical Baseline Scenario or a Common Practice Baseline 
Scenario. As explained earlier, timber harvesting in the natural forests of the YSFMA is managed by 
Rakyat Berjaya Sdn. Bhd while annual coupe permits are issued by the Sabah Forestry Department. 
Because of this system, there are no long-term harvest plans for the area that are being implemented and 
the implementation of the project is preventing the issuance of new coupe permits. In addition, the most 
likely baseline scenario includes the relatively new Mosaic Planting Approach. Because of the absence of 
the long-term management plan for Natural Forest Management and the fact that the Mosaic Planting 
Approach has not been applied yet in the project area, a Common Practice Baseline Scenario was applied 
to model the baseline scenario.

To ensure that the reference area includes the combination of the different forest management practices in

3.3.4 
Dissemination of Monitoring Plan and Results (CL4.2)

A series of brochures have been produced in the Malay language, which offer written summaries of 
the project objectives and implementing bodies and describe some of the underlying principles 
governing the project such biodiversity, carbon sequestration (including monitoring), global warming 
and the principles of FPIC.

Going forward, summary information of key project documents will be prepared in the Malay 
language and disseminated among communities in printed format. These will include the project PD 
(including the monitoring plan), monitoring reports, a schematic for the project’s grievance and 
redress mechanism, and any other appropriate documentation which may be requested by 
communities. The complete PD and the verified Monitoring Reports will be disseminated and made 
publicly available on the internet and this will ne communicated to the communities and other 
stakeholders through other means such as community notice boards as appropriate.

4.2.2 
Negative Community Impact Mitigation (CM2.2)

The Community Monitoring Plan will incorporate multiple indicators to capture and assess the magnitude of 
potential negative impacts. This method will be used in conjunction with other means such as community 
workshops, smaller group dialogues, the project grievance mechanism and general project-to-community 
lines of communication to both identify negative impacts as they arise and to formulate means of resolution 
in a participatory manner.

With respect to the specific risks outlined in Section 4.2.1, a number of measures will be employed from the 
beginning of implementation to minimize the probability of their manifestation. For the youth community 
group, it will be important to ensure that opportunities are presented for all interested group members to 
participate; within actualizable limits which are clearly established with communities from the outset. 
Activities are likely to begin relatively small, but scale-up and diversify as the project progresses. Regular 
dialogues will be held between affected community groups and project proponents to ensure that benefits 
are being distributed equitably, and to address any actual or nascent grievances.

4.4.1 
Community Monitoring Plan (CM4.1, CM4.2, GL1.4, GL2.2, GL2.3, GL2.5)

Monitoring of the impacts of project activities will be comprised of several mutually reinforcing methods 
which will be conducted over differing timescales. It is envisaged that a project Community Engagement 
Team will work with Project Zone communities over the long term in the implementation of project activities, 
and will also be responsible for the collection, collation and reporting of monitoring data. Methods to assess 
project impacts will include periodic household surveys, community-level engagements to assess project 
progress, smaller engagements targeting specific community groups, and communications via the 
grievance mechanism and other channels. Monitoring will thus constitute an ongoing aspect of project 
implementation, the results of which will be collated into regular (annual or biennial) monitoring reports.

Household surveys will be conducted among a randomly-selected sample of Project Zone community 
households every two years. These will aim to update the demographic and income baseline data reported 
in Section 4.1.1, and to record information related to impact indicators. Selected indicators will follow the

Information produced during the abovementioned monitoring activities will be collated and compiled into 
regular (annual or biennial) monitoring reports, which will contain the outputs of all monitoring activities 
(including potential negative impacts identified via the grievance mechanism), a synthesis of the data to 
assess to overall adherence of project activities and impacts to the Theory of Change, and revised activity 
plans for the mitigation of negative impacts and enhancement of positive impacts. Versions of the reports 
will be prepared in the Malay language and disseminated among Project Zone communities for validation.

The full monitoring plan (inclusive of timeframe, specific indicators, implementing personnel, reporting 
framework, budget etc.) will be prepared together with the implementation plan for project activities, and will 
be completed within 12 months of project validation (as specified in Richards and Panfil, 2011: p48).

4.4.2 
Monitoring Plan Dissemination (CM4.3)

Prior to the implementation of project activities, an Activity Implementation plan and the Community 
Monitoring Plan will be disseminated among the Project Zone communities in print form and in the Malay 
language. After an appropriate period of time for communities to read the documents and discuss them 
internally, the Community Engagement Team will hold dialogue sessions in communities to present the 
plans, discuss and receive feedback from community participants, and consequently make revisions to the 
plans as necessary.

The plans will be disseminated among other project stakeholders for inputs and proposed revisions. Once 
all stakeholders are satisfied with the plans, the finalized versions will be made publicly available on the 
project's website.

5.4.1 
Biodiversity Monitoring Plan (B4.1, B4.2, GL1.4, GL3.4)

Biodiversity monitoring activities are envisioned to be conducted together with the climate monitoring 
activities described in section 3.3.3, with collaboration from the Community Engagement team's monitoring 
activities described in section 4.4.1. All data collected, recorded, stored and reported will be subject to 
review and approval by team leaders and/or project managers with reference to written SOPs covering 
each level of data management. Local professional biologists and/or ecologists will also be consulted in the 
precise formulation of biodiversity monitoring methods and the evaluation of resultant data.

Indicators will include the pressure, state and response variables most relevant to biodiversity such as 
vegetation quality, presence of HCV 1 species, signs of anthropogenic disturbance, and the status of 
hunting activities. The project will explore the use of a recently developed smartphone-enabled tool for 
monitoring forest quality – the Forest Integrity Assessment (Suggit et al 2021)61.

The indicators used for carbon monitoring (through the monitoring of field plots and analysis of remotely-
sensed imagery) will track natural forest regeneration throughout the project's lifetime, which will provide a 
proxy measure for habitat health and suitability for RTE species. Signs of RTE species (direct sightings, 
tracks and/or scats) will be documented opportunistically by the field team during monthly surveillance and 
monitoring activities (see section 3.3.3), and recorded via data sheets, photographs, and GPS waypoints. 
Whilst these methods will not allow robust estimations of population densities, they are relatively cost-
effective and feasible within the overall project framework and will allow the determination of species 
presence and abundance indices for certain species. Signs of anthropogenic disturbance (such as 
vegetation cutting and used shotgun cartridges) will be similarly documented. The Community Engagement 
team will also address ongoing hunting as part of their monitoring activities.

All biodiversity monitoring data will be collated and analysed to produce annual reports which will track the 
efficacy of project interventions in safeguarding biodiversity and enhancing HCV 1 and HCV 2 values, and 
will include recommendations for more thorough research and potentially the adaptation of project activities 
should any negative trends be identified.

5.4.2 
Biodiversity Monitoring Plan Dissemination (B4.3)

The biodiversity monitoring plan will be disseminated among project stakeholders for inputs and proposed 
revisions. Once all stakeholders are satisfied with the plan, finalized versions will be made publicly 
available on the project's website together with periodic updates on monitoring outputs.

The project has sought to identify all stakeholders with a relationship to the project and to undertake an 
assessment of their rights, interests and relevance to the project itself. This assessment has included both 
institutional/non-community stakeholders (i.e. those with a relationship that is not simply based on proximity 
and/or use) and community stakeholders (those with a relationship based on proximity, tradition and/or 
current use).

Institutional/non-community stakeholders (such as, relevant governmental and non-governmental 
organisations) were initially identified through discussions with the principal project partners: the Sabah 
Forestry Department (SFD) and Yayasan Sabah/Rakyat Berjaya (RBJ). As a result of these discussions, 
the project initiated communications with those stakeholders responsible for the developmental 
administration of the project zone (including the District Office of Tongod) and NGOs with a history of 
community work in the area (including the PACOS Trust).

Local community stakeholders were identified through two main approaches: 1) through consultation with 
the institutional stakeholders (as above) to elicit information on communities with close linkages to the 
project area, and 2) by a spatial identification of all communities within an initial search radius of 20km from 
the project area boundary. This initial search identified a number of villages, and once permissions to 
engage with communities had been sought from the Tongod District Office, the project scheduled a series 
of preliminary meetings with the self-identified representatives of each community. During these meetings, 
the background and key objectives of the project were explained, and consent was sought to organise 
larger-scale workshops with a broad cross-section of community participants to explain the project in 
greater detail (inclusive of any potential risks which were apparent at the time). The workshops were also 
used as a means to assess general community interactions with/dependence on the project area, discuss 
the principal threats and challenges faced by communities, and seek further consent to proceed with 
project activities aimed at establishing social baseline conditions. This process resulted in the identification 
of eight communities as direct project stakeholders, all lying in close proximity to the norther boundary of 
the project area. A further two villages that lay on the periphery of the initial 20km search radius were not 
identified as stakeholders after further investigation. In one such village (Kg. Imbak) initial meetings with 
community representatives indicated clearly that the community identified no stake in the project area. In 
the other (Kg. Balat), the distance from the project area by boat (the only means of transport available) is 
almost 40km (despite the village lying on the edge of the 20km radius), and testimony from other project 
zone communities suggested that residents of this area seldom access the project area. Both villages will 
be contacted again as the project proceeds to re-evaluate their potential involvement. No other villages lay 
within the 20km initial search radius (including to the eastern, southern and western borders). As a result, 
the project zone, as defined by those communities identified as stakeholders, was identified as the area 
including only those eight villages living to the north along the banks of the Kinabatangan River.

2.1.9 
Stakeholder Descriptions (G1.6, G1.13)

The project is committed to protecting and enhancing the biodiversity value of the project area. Currently 
this is very high, with regionally significant populations of a number of important and threatened species, 
including orangutan, banteng, elephant, clouded leopard, sun bear, and bird species including Helmeted 
Hornbill, Storms Stork, Bornean Peacock Pheasant. Measures to monitor and enhance biodiversity value 
will centre around forest protection and control of hunting threats. Considerable effort will also be focused 
on monitoring, conducted by the project staff itself and coordinated by SEARRP, either routinely in 
conjunction with other activities, or on a periodic basis making use of temporary staff and local community 
members as required. In addition, the project will seek collaboration with other interested parties, including 
local academic institutions and research centres.

2.3.1 
Stakeholder Access to Project Documents (G3.1)

The Kuamut project has held a series of community engagements during which the project objectives and 
structure were explained and discussed. A series of brochures have been produced in the Malay language, 
which offer written summaries of the project objectives and implementing bodies and describe some of the 
underlying principles governing the project such as biodiversity, carbon sequestration, global warming and 
the principles of FPIC. These brochures have been given to community leaders were then asked to 
disseminate them amongst the wider community. The project will also provide access to documentation via 
the project website, and other means such as community notice boards as appropriate.

2.3.2 
Dissemination of Summary Project Documents (G3.1)

2.3.3 
Informational Meetings with Stakeholders (G3.1)

Since the inception of community engagements in late 2017, the project has held a total of 11 community 
workshops and dialogue sessions, attended by a combined total of 488 community participants. 
Community engagements are conducted to achieve a variety of objectives, including: transparency and 
communication of project details and activities, gathering information on community socio-cultural 
conditions and history, generation of spatial data via participatory mapping, discussion of threats and 
constraints faced by communities, and planning of future project activities in accordance with the principles 
of FPIC. Engagement sessions of this type are generally organised together with community leaders, who 
then publicise the engagements in their respective communities and encourage participation.

Furthermore, the project has conducted an extensive series of household surveys to provide data on the 
community socio-economic baseline. At the beginning of each individual interview conducted as part of 
these surveys, respondents are again given a brief overview of the project structure and objectives, and are 
asked for their consent before the interview proper is initiated.

As described in Section 2.3.3, the project has conducted 11 separate workshops and other meetings with 
village community stakeholders, reaching over 488 participants. A full list of such meetings is provided in 
Table 4 in Section 2.3.3. During these engagement events, frequent discussion sessions are held in which 
community members are asked to give input concerning the most appropriate forms of assistance the 
project could potentially offer – indeed all the activities mentioned in Section 2.1.11 are derived from 
discussions with (and data provided by) the communities themselves and are not imposed by the project. 
Moreover, the project seeks to ensure that all potential activities are designed specifically for each 
individual community; recognising inter-community diversity in terms of aspirations and the suitability of 
different interventions.

2.3.8 
Continued Consultation and Adaptive Management (G3.4)

As above, the project community engagement process focuses on regular workshops and meetings during 
which community participants are encouraged to shape how engagements should be conducted in the 
future - establishing an iterative process in which the structure of engagements is predicated both on 
project needs and community preferences. The project will continue to conduct community interactions in a 
flexible and responsive manner, responding to changing community circumstances by adapting project 
activities and modes of engagement.

2.3.9 
Stakeholder Consultation Channels (G3.5)

Engagements have been conducted via a number of fora, including community workshops and informal 
meetings with community leaders. In addition, the team has established a social media discussion group 
with leaders of all Project Zone communities to facilitate communication relating to project activities. The 
Kuamut project continues to hold regular community engagements during which the project objectives and 
structure are explained and discussed. A series of brochures have been produced in the Malay language, 
which offer written summaries of the project objectives and implementing bodies and describe some of the 
underlying principles governing the project such biodiversity, carbon sequestration, global warming and the 
principles of FPIC. These brochures have been given to community leaders who are then asked to 
disseminate them amongst the wider community. The project will also provide access to documentation via 
the project website, and other means such as community notice boards as appropriate.
2.3.10 Stakeholder Participation in Decision-Making and Implementation (G3.6)

Meeting types, structure and locations are always designed to enable the target audience to participate 
freely and to contribute openly. Importantly, all engagements are conducted in the communities themselves 
at venues considered appropriate by community leaders. Community members are never asked to travel 
outside of their villages in order to participate in project engagements.

Although organising attendance of community members at workshops is left to the discretion of community 
leaders, they are encouraged to ensure that a broad cross-section of the community is represented – in 
particular women and youth groups which may be under-represented otherwise. They are also encouraged 
to make sure that as many people as possible attend workshops in order to maximise the direct outreach 
between the project and individual community members.

As the project progresses and community groups become more clearly defined, additional efforts will be 
made to hold dialogues specifically tailored to each group in order to facilitate candid (or even anonymous) 
communication with project staff.

arising from project zone communities or other stakeholders. In the community context, procedures are

and monitoring as well as engagement with communities.

Furthermore, the project is implemented jointly with the South East Asia Rainforest Research Partnership

The community work is implemented jointly with PACOS Trust (https://pacostrust.com/), a community-

2.4.4 
Project Management Partnerships/Team Development (G4.2)

The project area is legally owned by the Sabah State Government which excludes any territory from 
indigenous or local communities. The necessary rights to implement the Kuamut Conservation Project were 
provided to the project proponent through an agreement between Permian Malaysia, the State Government 
of Sabah and Rakyat Berjaya SDN, BHD. Copy of this agreement is available for the review of the auditors.

The project has generated an initial overview of community lands and resource use areas outside the 
project area through the process of participatory mapping. Tenurial insecurity is one of the most significant 
challenges faced by members of the project zone communities; as is the case for most rural indigenous 
peoples in Sabah. Land in the state is alienated to indigenous peoples under the Sabah Land Ordinance in 
the form of a documentary title referred to as Native Title (NT). The process of applying for lands via the 
designated State authority (the Department of Lands and Survey) is historically fraught with difficulty, and 
many community members continue to await the issuance of formal land titles for long periods of time – 
sometimes decades. Moreover, official cadastral maps of land titles are not publicly available in Sabah and 
are considered confidential government documents. These issues constitute an obvious impediment to the 
production of spatially accurate maps of land tenure in the project zone. Nonetheless, approximate maps of 
community settlement areas, agricultural lands, areas accessed for harvesting natural resources and 
culturally significant sites have been produced through participatory mapping processes with communities. 
Moreover, communities have been made aware repeatedly during engagements that the project area 
corresponds to the boundaries of the Northern Kuamut forest reserve and that project activities relating to 
the maintenance and enhancement of climate and biodiversity benefits will take place solely within the 
project area. Any customary rights of the local communities will be respected through the project 
implementation which can be confirmed at each verification period.

2.5.2 
Recognition of Property Rights (G5.1)

As described in the previous section, the project is implemented respecting all property rights which were 
transferred to Permian Malaysia through an agreement signed with the Sabah State Government.

The topic of disputes over lands and resources has been discussed during community engagements on 
multiple occasions. Some parts of the project area are considered by communities to be part of their 
ancestral lands and remain of importance for the gathering of natural resources. Many community 
members feel that their rights to access and use natural resources have been circumscribed by the 
gazettement of the Kuamut forest reserve – and indeed these activities are not considered lawful under the 
Sabah Forestry Department’s legislation. These are issues concerning which the project will endeavour to 
facilitate agreements between government and community stakeholders which are congruent with 
biodiversity conservation, climate change mitigation, community livelihoods and State law. As the project 
matures and grows, it will adopt formal Standard Operating Procedures governing staff conduct with

respect to community engagement founded on FPIC principles. The project will also negotiate written 
agreements with communities which will serve as guiding documents for future project-community 
collaborations.

2.5.3 
Free, Prior and Informed Consent (G5.2)

The Kuamut project views Free, Prior and Informed Consent (FPIC) as a set of guiding principles rather 
that a specific methodology, and adopts a procedural conception of FPIC which is consistent with 
prominent contemporary literature and best-practices on the subject (e.g. Colchester 20104; Anderson 
20115; FAO 20146).

All forms of community-project interactions are informed and governed by FPIC principles. Open and 
transparent discussions are held during all engagement activities, during which communities are 
encouraged to voice any concerns they may have over the project without fear of censure. Any and all 
activities proposed by the project are discussed with communities far in advance of any potential 
implementation, and communities are given opportunities to discuss among themselves and raise 
objections as they feel appropriate. Consent is considered to be fluid and multi-faceted, and is repeatedly 
sought at multiple stages (e.g. before commencing social entry, before conducting community workshops, 
before commencing data gathering activities such as household surveys). Moreover, the concept of FPIC 
as adopted by the project is explained in project documentation such as brochures, in order to ensure that 
the communities themselves are aware of their rights to receive clear and transparent information on the 
project, and to withhold consent if they feel it appropriate to do so.

The topic of disputes over lands and resources has been discussed during community engagements on 
multiple occasions. Some parts of the project area are considered by communities to be part of their 
ancestral lands and remain of importance for the gathering of natural resources (broadly indicated by the 
HCV 5 and 6 areas in the maps in Section 2.1.7. Many community members feel that their rights to access 
and use natural resources have been circumscribed by the gazettement of the Kuamut forest reserve – and 
indeed these activities are not considered lawful under the Sabah Forestry Department’s legislation. These 
are issues concerning which the project will endeavour to facilitate agreements between government and 
community stakeholders which are congruent with biodiversity conservation, climate change mitigation, 
community livelihoods and State law.

However, although community access rights to traditional lands and resources remains a contentious issue 
(and one which will require considerable future efforts from all parties to ameliorate), it does not at present 
constitute a source of disputes per se. At the time of writing, the project is not aware of any disputes over 
lands or resources (whether current or in the recent past) which have involved legal arbitration, protest, or 
any form of physical or verbal conflict. This situation will constantly be monitored as part of the 
implementation of the community engagement plan to be developed prior to first verification of the project.

The success of community programs are largely dependent on participation, transparent decision-
making processes based on mutual trust, and proper management of project activities. Three main 
potential barriers to community benefits in reaching the marginalized and/or vulnerable communities 
were identified during the social survery, and mitigation measures are presented in the diagram and 
discussed below.

Lack of participation: The marginalized poor communities tend to live remotely away from village 
centres, and often lack the means or time required to attend community meetings, due to distance 
and other constraints. Also, it is common for the project-zone communities that the marginalized feel 
discouraged to voice their opinions in front of dominant groups. This can trigger mistrust toward other 
community members and leads to lack of motivation and willingness to participate. Also, unbalanced 
or misrepresented target groups for certain project activities could entail non-participation of the 
poorer and marginalized community members. The Kuamut Project will encourage all community 
stakeholders, particularly the poorer and marginalized, to participate in project activities through 
differentiated approaches. The participatory planning processes enables all project-zone communities 
to be involved in decision-makings. Understanding barriers to meaningful participation to the project, 
socialization, information dissemination and community meetings take place at various locations and 
times by considering the needs of the marginalized. For example, some meetings will be facilitated 
only for women, and take place at their houses in the evening when they usually have spare time. 
Community message boards, booklets, flyers and videos, and local radio programs could also be 
used to reach target audience effectively.

Elite captures: A lack of participation and transparency in decision-making processes generally 
creates an opportunity for elite captures in which dominant groups can steer decisions to their favour, 
while hindering the flow of benefits to the marginalized households. When making decisions 
regarding an infrastructural development project such as road construction, for example, community 
board members may choose a location based on their personal benefits, rather than communal 
benefits as a whole. Without transparent decision-making systems and well-represented board of 
communities in place, community programs may be manipulated to satisfy the personal interests of 
certain individuals and may not produce overall positive impacts on the marginalized households. In 
order to address the risk of elite captures, the Kuamut Project will encourage the poorer and 
marginalized communities to participate (see above) and aim to enhance the balance of community 
representation. To increase transparency in decision-making processes of the activities to be 
undertaken with the communities, meeting records and decisions will be maintained and made 
publicly available. A mixed representation of community members, including the marginalized groups, 
will reinforce more equitable and democratic distribution of benefits, thereby placing checks and 
balances on decision-making processes and safeguarding the interest of communities as a whole.

Improper management of project activities: Another potential barrier to anticipated project benefits 
reaching target community members is improper management of project activities due to the lack of 
human and financial resources and effective monitoring and evaluation systems. The implementation 
and progress of project activities with the communities should be regularly monitored in order to 
assess the impacts of these activities on the marginalized households, to ensure appropriate 
allocation and use of community funds, and to enforce rules. Without a stringent system of checks 
and balances, the risk of the elite capture of benefits, ineffective performance and misappropriation of 
funds remains high. Proper training will also be provided to build the capacity of local people. 
Community-based adaptive management plan will reinforce checks and balances on decision-making 
processes and lead to a form of democratic natural resources governance.

Through the socio-economic survey, the project team was able to identify the priorities that members
